note: First Activity Library batch. AI-drafted against the plan 2.1 rubric; nothing publishes without Matthew's approval in the review queue.

activities.title: Follow the Scarf
activities.intention: Give young eyes practice following a slow-moving object, the groundwork for visual tracking.

materials.item: a light scarf or muslin cloth

steps: Lie your baby on their back and hold the scarf about a foot above them.
Float it slowly from one side to the other. Watch their eyes follow.
Pause in the middle. Lower it a little and let them find your face.
Let the scarf drift down onto your hand. Say: "There it goes!"
activities.adapt_down: Move slower and keep the scarf closer to the middle, where looking is easiest.
activities.adapt_up: Trace a gentle circle, or float it just out of view and back.
activities.evidence_note: Following slow movement with the eyes is early practice for the looking skills reading builds on later.
activities.safety_notes: Keep the scarf in your hands, and put it away when the game ends.

activities.title: The Kitchen Narrator
activities.intention: Bathe your baby in warm, responsive talk during a chore you were doing anyway.

materials.item: whatever you are already cooking or washing

steps: Set your baby somewhere they can see you work.
Narrate what you do in a warm, sing-song voice: "Now we wash the apple. Cold water!"
When your baby coos or kicks, stop and answer them: "Oh, you think so?"
Wait a beat after you speak. The pause invites their turn.
activities.adapt_down: Shorten the sentences and lean closer, so your face does half the talking.
activities.adapt_up: Name what your baby is looking at, not just what you are holding.
activities.evidence_note: Back-and-forth exchanges, even with a baby who cannot talk yet, are among the strongest known supports for language growth.
activities.safety_notes: Keep your baby's seat well back from the stove and counter edges.

activities.title: Tummy Time with a Mirror Friend
activities.intention: Make tummy time worth the effort by giving the push-up a fascinating reward: a face.
steps: Place your baby on their tummy facing a mirror, on a firm blanket.
Get down on the floor beside them so your face appears too.
Talk to the baby in the mirror: "Who is that? There you are!"
When the effort turns to fussing, end on a win. Roll them over and celebrate.
activities.adapt_down: Prop their chest on a rolled towel so lifting the head takes less work.
activities.adapt_up: Slide the mirror slightly to one side so they turn and reach toward it.
activities.evidence_note: Tummy time builds the neck and trunk strength that sitting, crawling, and reaching all draw on.
activities.safety_notes: Stay on the floor with your baby for all of tummy time.

activities.title: The Great Drop Game
activities.intention: Turn the maddening high-chair drop into a lesson in cause and effect and conversation.

materials.item: a soft toy or silicone cup

steps: When your baby drops the cup from the high chair, make it an event: "Boom! It fell DOWN."
Pick it up slowly and set it back. Wait, and watch their face.
When it goes over again, act amazed again. Same words, same drama.
After a few rounds, pause before returning it. Let them ask with a look or a sound.
activities.adapt_down: Drop it yourself first and narrate, so the pattern comes before the job.
activities.adapt_up: Offer two things and name which one fell: "The CUP fell. The spoon stayed."
activities.evidence_note: Repeating an action to reproduce its effect is how babies test that their actions move the world.
activities.safety_notes: Use soft or unbreakable droppables only.

activities.title: Half-Hidden Treasure
activities.intention: Practice holding a vanished toy in mind, the beginning of object permanence.
steps: Show the toy, then slide it halfway under the blanket while they watch.
Ask: "Where did it go?" and wait for the grab.
Cheer the find. Next round, cover a little more of it.
When full hiding works, hide it under one of two blankets.
activities.adapt_down: Leave most of the toy showing, and lift the blanket together.
activities.adapt_up: Hide it fully, count to two, then let them search.
activities.evidence_note: Searching for a fully hidden object marks a real step in memory for things out of sight.
activities.safety_notes: Choose a toy larger than your baby's mouth.

activities.title: Banana Pincer Picnic
activities.intention: Give the emerging thumb-and-finger grip a soft, tasty job it can win.
steps: Cut soft banana into pieces about the size of your fingertip.
Scatter three or four on the tray. Fewer is better for focus.
Let them work at picking each one up. No helping hands.
Name the win: "You got it! Right in your fingers."
activities.adapt_down: Use slightly bigger, stickier pieces that are easier to trap.
activities.adapt_up: Offer pieces one at a time from your flat palm, or add a soft pea-sized target.
activities.evidence_note: The thumb-and-forefinger pickup is a fine-motor milestone that self-feeding practices better than any toy.
activities.safety_notes: Serve soft foods in fingertip-sized pieces, and stay at the table during eating.

activities.title: Pots-and-Pans Copy Band
activities.intention: Trade rhythms back and forth, so listening and copying become a game.
steps: Give each of you a pot and a spoon.
Tap a simple beat: tap-tap. Then hold your spoon still and wait.
Whatever they play back, copy it exactly. Their turn leads now.
Trade leader and copier a few times. End with one big finale tap.
activities.adapt_down: Hold their hand and tap together first, so the copy starts in their body.
activities.adapt_up: Play tap-TAP loud-soft patterns, or add a pause inside the beat.
activities.evidence_note: Copying and being copied teaches the give-and-take structure that conversation is built on.

activities.title: Sock Basket In and Out
activities.intention: Practice hearing a small ask and doing it, inside a real job with a clear finish.
steps: Tip the socks out. Name the job: "Socks go IN!"
Hand socks over one at a time. Say "in" as each lands.
When the basket is full, flip it: "Now they come OUT!"
Try small asks: "Put it in." "Take one out." "Give it to me."
activities.adapt_down: Do the first few hand-over-hand, then let go.
activities.adapt_up: Try a two-part ask: "Take one out, then give it to Papa."
activities.evidence_note: Doing small spoken asks inside a routine is where a child's grasp of words first shows.

activities.title: The Point-and-Name Walk
activities.intention: Follow your child's point and name what caught their eye, right when they care most.

materials.item: a stroller or carrier, or just shoes

steps: Walk slowly. Let your child set what matters.
When they point, look where the finger goes and name it: "A bus! A big bus."
Add one detail, then stop talking: "The bus is loud."
Point at things yourself too, and wait to see if they look.
activities.adapt_down: Name whatever they stare at, even without a point. Staring counts.
activities.adapt_up: Ask a tiny question after naming: "Where did the bus go?"
activities.evidence_note: Naming exactly what a child is attending to is one of the best-timed language gifts a parent can give.

activities.title: Add-a-Word Echo
activities.intention: Stretch one-word tries into two-word phrases by echoing back a little more.
steps: When your child says a word, say it back warmly with one word added: "Dog!" becomes "Big dog!"
Keep your voice curious, not corrective. You are agreeing, not fixing.
Pause after your echo. Sometimes they take the longer phrase for a spin.
Sprinkle this through the day. Three or four echoes beat one long drill.
activities.adapt_down: Echo their sounds and gestures the same way: point plus word.
activities.adapt_up: Add describing words or little verbs: "Dog running! Wet dog."
activities.evidence_note: Expanding on a child's own words is a well-tested strategy speech therapists teach parents first.

activities.title: Cushion Mountain
activities.intention: Build climbing, balance, and body planning on a mountain that forgives every fall.
steps: Pile cushions into a low mountain on a carpet, away from table corners.
Drape the blanket over it so surfaces shift a little underfoot.
Invite the climb: up, over, and roll down the far side.
Rebuild it a new way each round. New mountain, new plan.
activities.adapt_down: Keep the pile one cushion high and hold a hand for the first trips.
activities.adapt_up: Add a carry job: bring the teddy to the top, then back down.
activities.evidence_note: Climbing over uneven, shifting surfaces builds the balance reactions flat floors never ask for.
activities.safety_notes: Keep the pile low, clear hard edges from the landing zone, and stay beside the mountain.

activities.title: The Spoon-and-Sock Sort
activities.intention: Practice grouping things by kind, the quiet start of thinking in categories.
steps: Mix spoons and socks in one heap. Set out two bowls.
Sort the first two yourself, thinking out loud: "Spoons here. Socks there."
Hand items over one at a time and let them choose the bowl.
Wrong bowl? Just narrate it: "A spoon with the socks! It wants its friends."
activities.adapt_down: Use two things that look wildly different, like spoons and teddy bears.
activities.adapt_up: Sort the same pile a new way: big things and little things.
activities.evidence_note: Sorting by kind shows a child is grouping the world into concepts, not just handling objects.

activities.title: Ready, Set... Wait!
activities.intention: Practice putting the brakes on a body that wants to go, which is harder than going.
steps: Stand together at a start line. Build it up: "Ready... set..."
Sometimes say "GO!" and race. Sometimes whisper "...wait!" and freeze.
Make the wait funny: tiptoe tall, hold your breath, wiggle only one finger.
Let them be the caller for you. Freezing YOU is the best part.
activities.adapt_down: Keep waits very short, one second, and always end in a GO.
activities.adapt_up: Stretch the wait, or add a rule: go slow like a snail until GO.
activities.evidence_note: Stopping an action mid-impulse is early self-control practice, and games are where it grows best.

activities.title: The Oat Pour Station
activities.intention: Give hands rich pouring and scooping practice with a material that sweeps right up.

materials.item: dry oats in a big bowl
cups, scoops, and a muffin tin

steps: Set the big bowl of oats on a tray with cups and scoops.
Show one good pour, slow and high, so the oats whisper down.
Hand it over and narrate what their hands do: full, empty, more, all gone.
End with the cleanup pour: everything back in the big bowl.
activities.adapt_down: Use big scoops and a wide bowl, and let hands do the scooping first.
activities.adapt_up: Add a target: fill each muffin-tin cup exactly to the top.
activities.evidence_note: Pouring and scooping build the wrist and grip control that later hold pencils steady.
activities.safety_notes: Stay at the table during play, and sweep strays so the floor is not slippery.

activities.title: The Feelings Photo Tour
activities.intention: Put names on feelings while looking at the faces your child knows best.

materials.item: family photos on your phone or a picture book

steps: Snuggle up and look at photos of people your child loves.
Name what faces show: "Grandma is laughing. She feels happy."
Find a grumpy or teary face too. Those get names without any fixing.
Ask gently: "Where is the happy one?" and let them hunt.
activities.adapt_down: Stick to happy and sad, the two easiest to spot.
activities.adapt_up: Wonder about causes: "Why is he sad? His ice cream fell!"
activities.evidence_note: Children who hear feelings named learn faster to manage their own.

activities.title: The What-Happens-Next Pause
activities.intention: Turn story time into story-building by handing your child the next page before you turn it.
steps: Read as usual until something is about to happen.
Stop with your hand on the page: "Uh oh. What happens NEXT?"
Take any answer seriously, wild ones especially. Then turn and find out.
At the end, ask for the story back: "What happened to the bear?"
activities.adapt_down: Offer two choices: "Does he hide, or does he jump?"
activities.adapt_up: Pause before the last page and invent a different ending together.
activities.evidence_note: Predicting and retelling turn a child from a listener into a storyteller, which feeds later reading.

activities.title: Tape Line Trails
activities.intention: Lay a floor trail that asks the body to balance, plan, and follow two-part directions.
steps: Tape a trail on the floor: straight bits, zigzags, a circle island.
Walk it together first, heel to toe, arms out like wings.
Add moves: jump the gap, tiptoe the zigzag, spin on the island.
Give two-part missions: "Walk the line, THEN hop to the circle."
activities.adapt_down: Make the lines wide and straight, and hold a hand for the first laps.
activities.adapt_up: Walk it backward, or balance a beanbag-sized soft toy on one palm.
activities.evidence_note: Narrow-path walking and two-step directions each stretch a three-year-old just past easy, where growth lives.
activities.safety_notes: Lay the trail on grippy flooring away from furniture corners.

activities.title: Switch-the-Sort Treasure Tray
activities.intention: Sort one tray of treasures two different ways, so thinking learns to change the rule.

materials.item: a tray of safe household objects, like lids, spoons, and blocks

steps: Gather a tray of objects that differ in kind, size, and color.
Round one: sort by kind. Lids together, spoons together.
Mix it all back up with ceremony. That part is fun on purpose.
Round two, new rule: "Now BIG things here, LITTLE things there."
activities.adapt_down: Stay with one rule until it is easy, and sort only six objects.
activities.adapt_up: Let them invent round three's rule, and you guess what it is.
activities.evidence_note: Switching sorting rules is a classic test of flexible thinking, and playing it is practicing it.
activities.safety_notes: Choose objects too big to swallow.
